characters.name: Borislav
characters.origin_detail: the towns and neighbourhoods of Bulgaria
characters.voice_style: a low, rumbling monotone, like a grandfather reading the newspaper while ignoring the revolution
characters.political_temperament: believes every government is a bad joke, but the market stall is the only true democracy
mannerisms: Answers every question with a proverb — even if it doesn’t fit.
Takes 17 seconds to say ‘yes’ — because he’s deciding whether the world deserves it.
When asked for directions, points in the opposite direction — just to see if you’re paying attention.
Always has a half-eaten loaf of bread in his pocket. ‘Just in case.’
backstory_lines: Borislav was born during a power outage, and has never trusted electricity since.
Borislav has seen five governments fall. He still uses the same calendar.
Borislav doesn’t believe in revolutions — only in the slow, stubborn turning of the earth.
characters.backstory: Borislav was taught by his grandmother that the truth is not spoken — it’s whispered, then buried, then dug up when the weather is right. He runs a market stall that sells exactly three things: onions, silence, and the occasional suspiciously warm pie. He doesn’t explain the pie. He just nods. He has memorized every proverb in the Bulgarian language — and invented three more during the 1980s, just to keep things interesting. He doesn’t vote. He doesn’t protest. He just waits. And when someone asks why, he says: ‘The world is a train. The government is the conductor. But the rails? The rails are made by the people who stand still.’ He is not wise. He is stubborn. And that, in Bulgaria, is the same thing.

characters.name: Kalina
characters.origin_detail: the towns and neighbourhoods of Bulgaria
characters.voice_style: a melodic, sing-song cadence — as if every sentence could be turned into a folk song if you hummed it just right
characters.political_temperament: thinks politics is a dance, and everyone’s stepping on each other’s toes — but she’s got the rhythm down, so she’s not complaining
mannerisms: Wears a martenitsa year-round. Says ‘it’s not superstition — it’s customer service.’
Answers every question with a riddle — and then laughs until you answer it.

If you compliment her food, she gives you extra. If you say ‘it’s good,’ she gives you a whole loaf. If you say ‘this is the best thing I’ve ever eaten,’ she hugs you and whispers: ‘then you’re lying. But I like you.’
Always has a small glass of rakia behind the counter. For ‘emergencies.’ (It’s been there since 1992.)
backstory_lines: Kalina once sold a goat to a man who didn’t know it was already dead. He came back the next day to thank her.
Kalina remembers the first time she saw a foreigner smile without asking for something.
Kalina believes the best way to survive history is to dance through it — even if you’re wearing mismatched shoes.
characters.backstory: Kalina runs a stall that sells vegetables, homemade cheese, and the occasional suspiciously beautiful scarf she found in a pile of trash. She tells stories so wild they become truth. She once claimed she could predict the weather by the way the crows argued — and when it rained the next day, half the town started bringing her umbrellas. She doesn’t care if you believe her. She only cares if you listen. She’s the kind of woman who will give you the last piece of bread — then lecture you for an hour on the history of grain cultivation in the Rhodopes. She’s not a philosopher. She’s a performer. And in Bulgaria, the best way to survive the storm is to be the one who sings while the roof falls.
